src: お世話になっております
ja: お世話になっております
kana: おせわになっております
english: thanks for your continued support (business greeting)
use: Opens almost every work phone call or email to a client or partner; the other side answers kochira koso osewa ni natte orimasu.

example.romaji: itsumo osewa ni natte orimasu. tanaka desu.
example.ja: いつもお世話になっております。田中です。
example.english: Hello, it's Tanaka. Thanks as always for your support.

notes: The past form osewa ni narimashita thanks someone who looked after you, e.g. when you leave a host family or a job.

use: Polite lead-in before asking a client, staff member or stranger to do something; common in business emails, on forms and in announcements.

example.romaji: otesuu desu ga, kochira ni onamae o onegai shimasu.
example.ja: お手数ですが、こちらにお名前をお願いします。
example.english: Sorry to trouble you, but could you write your name here?

notes: Otesuu o okake shimasu means sorry for the trouble I'm causing. With friends say warui kedo instead.

kana: ただいまもどりました
use: Said on walking back into the office after going out; colleagues answer okaerinasai or otsukaresama desu.

example.ja: ただいま戻りました。何かありましたか？
example.english: I'm back. Did anything come up?

notes: At home just say tadaima.

english: what do you want to do?; what shall we do?
use: Asks a friend to decide or pick between options; answer with your choice plus ni suru, or dotchi demo ii.

example.romaji: ame da kedo, dou suru? ie de eiga miru?
example.ja: 雨だけど、どうする？家で映画見る？
example.english: It's raining. What do you want to do? Watch a movie at home?

examplePolite.romaji: ame desu ne. dou shimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨ですね。どうしますか？
examplePolite.english: It's raining. What shall we do?

notes: Dou shiyou (what do I do?) is the worried version you say to yourself.

use: Soft, homey request to family and close friends, after a thing (sore choudai) or a -te verb (matte choudai).

example.ja: それちょうだい！喉渇いた。
example.english: Give me that! I'm thirsty.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、それをください。

notes: Can sound childlike or motherly; adults asking strangers use kudasai.

use: Said with confidence when you take on a job someone is worried about.

example.ja: 料理？任せて！得意だから。
example.english: Cooking? Leave it to me, I'm good at it.

examplePolite.romaji: sono ken wa watashi ni makasete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: その件は私に任せてください。

notes: Makaseru means to entrust. Omakase at a sushi bar means chef's choice.

politeJa: どうしたらいいですか
use: Asks someone for advice when you're stuck or don't know the next step.

example.ja: 鍵なくしちゃった。どうしたらいい？
example.english: I lost my keys. What should I do?

examplePolite.romaji: kagi o nakushite shimatta n desu ga, dou shitara ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 鍵をなくしてしまったんですが、どうしたらいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I've lost my key. What should I do?

notes: Dou sureba ii? means the same.

use: Presses a request on a friend or junior, or tells them you're relying on them; the answer is makasete.

example.ja: 明日の準備、頼むよ。
example.english: I'm counting on you to get things ready for tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no junbi, onegai shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の準備、お願いしますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll leave tomorrow's prep to you, then.

notes: Women usually say onegai ne instead.

english: are you sure?; is it really okay?
use: Checks that someone means it when they offer you something or do you a favour; follow with thanks.

example.ja: え、おごり？いいの？
example.english: Wait, your treat? Are you sure?

examplePolite.romaji: e, ii n desu ka? arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: え、いいんですか？ありがとうございます。
examplePolite.english: Oh, are you sure? Thank you.

notes: Also asks permission after a -te verb: kore tabete ii no? (can I eat this?).

use: An eager yes to an invitation or a request for help.

example.romaji: sasotte kurete arigatou. yorokonde iku yo!
example.ja: 誘ってくれてありがとう。喜んで行くよ！
example.english: Thanks for inviting me. I'd love to come!

examplePolite.ja: 喜んでお手伝いします。

notes: Some izakaya staff shout hai, yorokonde! when they take an order.

use: Asks permission or checks something is fine; put the thing first (koko, ii desu ka?) or a -te mo verb (suwatte mo ii desu ka?).

example.romaji: sumimasen, koko suwatte mo ii desu ka?
example.ja: すみません、ここ座ってもいいですか？
example.english: Excuse me, is it okay if I sit here?

notes: Casual is just ii? with a rising tone. Yes is hai, douzo; a no usually starts with chotto...

use: Desperate or exasperated plea to a friend or family member to stop or do something.

example.ja: 頼むから、もうやめて。
example.english: Please, I'm begging you, just stop.

notes: Stronger than tanomu yo. Onegai dakara is the softer version anyone can use.

use: Softens a favour or a no to a friend; say it first, then the request or refusal.

example.ja: 悪いけど、窓閉めてくれる？
example.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen ga, mado o shimete moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: すみませんが、窓を閉めてもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you close the window?

notes: Warui ne afterwards means sorry about that.

use: Emotional plea, usually before stop, listen or don't go.

example.ja: お願いだから、話聞いて。
example.english: Please, just listen to me.

examplePolite.ja: お願いですから、やめてください。

notes: Softer than tanomu kara and used by everyone.

use: Firm, polite no to staff, salespeople or a host offering more; add iie or a reason to sound warmer.

example.romaji: iie, kekkou desu. mou juubun itadakimashita.
example.ja: いいえ、結構です。もう十分いただきました。
example.english: No, thank you. I've had plenty.

notes: Can sound cold to friends; use daijoubu instead. Kekkou also means quite: kekkou oishii (pretty tasty).

use: Agrees to a plan someone just suggested.

example.ja: いいね、そうしよう！
example.english: Good idea, let's do that!

examplePolite.ja: いいですね。そうしましょう。

notes: Sou suru (I'll do that) is for your own plan only.

english: would that be all right?; may I?
use: Very polite ii desu ka; you hear it from staff checking an order, and can use it with bosses and strangers.

example.ja: こちらでよろしいですか？
example.english: Will this one be all right?

notes: Staff also say yoroshii deshou ka, softer still.

use: Lead-in before a personal or awkward question.

example.romaji: chotto kiite mo ii? kanojo iru?
example.ja: ちょっと聞いてもいい？彼女いる？
example.english: Can I ask you something? Do you have a girlfriend?

examplePolite.romaji: hitotsu kiite mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 一つ聞いてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Can I ask you one thing?

notes: Very polite version: ukagatte mo yoroshii desu ka.

english: would you like some?; how about it?; how is it?
use: Polite offer or check-in from staff or a host (fukuro wa ikaga desu ka?); answer onegai shimasu or daijoubu desu.

example.romaji: koohii no okawari, ikaga desu ka?
example.ja: コーヒーのおかわり、いかがですか？
example.english: Would you like more coffee?

notes: Casual version: dou? Staff also say ikaga deshou ka, and ikaga deshita ka (how was it?).

english: shall I help?; want a hand?
use: Offers help to someone carrying, cooking or struggling with something.

example.ja: 重そうだね。手伝おうか？
example.english: That looks heavy. Want a hand?

examplePolite.ja: 重そうですね。手伝いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: That looks heavy. Shall I help?

notes: Humbler still: otetsudai shimashou ka. Nanika tetsudau? means anything I can do?
